## Preliminary Steps
```{r}
# Load necessary packages
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)
library(sf)
library(tmap)
```

```{r}
# Load/read in the necessary data
ejscreen <- st_read("data/ejscreen/EJSCREEN_2023_BG_StatePct_with_AS_CNMI_GU_VI.gdb")
crashes <- read_csv("data/ejscreen/SWITRS_LA/Crashes.csv")
holc <- st_read("data/ejscreen/mapping-inequality/mapping-inequality-los-angeles.json")
```


## Part 1: Legacy of redlining in current environmental (in)justice

### (a). Create a map of historical redlining neighborhoods

```{r}
# Filter to data of interest
la <- ejscreen |> 
      dplyr::filter(CNTY_NAME == "Los Angeles County") 
la_shape <- st_as_sf(la)
holc_shape <- st_as_sf(holc)
```

```{r}
# Make the map!
tmap_mode("view")
la_map <- tm_shape(la_shape) +
    tm_polygons() +
    tm_shape(holc_shape) +
    tm_polygons(fill = "grade", fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "HOLC Grade")) +
    tm_title(text = "HOLC Redlining Grades for Los Angeles County", size = 1.1, fontface = "bold", position = tm_pos_out("center", "top"), frame = TRUE)
la_map
```

### (b). Table summarizing the percentage of census block groups that fall within each HOLC grade

```{r}
# First we need to combine the EJScreen and HOLC data spatially
# We need to make sure the CRS match!
if(st_crs(ejscreen) == st_crs(holc)){
  print("CRS match")
}else{
  print("CRS do not match")
}
```

```{r}
# The CRS do not match, so we need to transform one of the datasets so that they match
holc_transformed <- st_transform(holc, crs = st_crs(ejscreen))

# Check that the CRS now match
if(st_crs(ejscreen) == st_crs(holc_transformed)){
  print("CRS match")
}else{
  print("CRS do not match")
}
```

```{r}
# The CRS now match, so we can now join the datasets
# We only care about the LA data from EJScreen
ej_and_holc <- st_join(la, holc_transformed, join = st_intersects)

# Now that the data is joined, we can drop geometries
ej_and_holc <- st_drop_geometry(ej_and_holc)
```

```{r}
# Make summary table
summ_table <- ej_and_holc |> 
    count(grade) |> 
    mutate(percentage = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 1))
print(summ_table)
```


### (c). Visualizations summarizing current conditions within HOLC grades for % low income, percentile for Particulate Matter 2.5, and percentile for low life expectancy

```{r}
# First take the means of these variables, grouped by HOLC grade
holc_vars_summ <- ej_and_holc |> 
    group_by(grade) |> 
    summarize(mean(P_LOWINCPCT, na.rm = TRUE), mean(P_PM25, na.rm = TRUE), mean(P_LIFEEXPPCT, na.rm = TRUE))
```

```{r}
# Visualize as a scatterplot!
# Need to pivot longer first so we have one row per grade/variable combo
holcvars_long <- holc_vars_summ |> 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(`mean(P_LOWINCPCT, na.rm = TRUE)`, `mean(P_PM25, na.rm = TRUE)`, `mean(P_LIFEEXPPCT, na.rm = TRUE)`),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "percentile"
  )

ggplot(holcvars_long, aes(x = grade, y = percentile, color = variable)) +
    geom_point() +
    scale_color_discrete(
        labels = c(
            `mean(P_LOWINCPCT, na.rm = TRUE)` = "% Low Income", 
            `mean(P_PM25, na.rm = TRUE)` = "PM2.5 Exposure", 
            `mean(P_LIFEEXPPCT, na.rm = TRUE)` = "Life Expectancy")
    ) +
    labs(x = "HOLC Grade", y = "Percentile", color = NULL)
```

```{r}
# We can also visualize individual variables with barplots
# Life expectancy
holc_lifeexp <- ej_and_holc |> 
    group_by(grade) |> 
    summarize(mean(P_LIFEEXPPCT, na.rm = TRUE))
life_exp_plot <- ggplot(holc_lifeexp, aes(x = grade, y = `mean(P_LIFEEXPPCT, na.rm = TRUE)`)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
    labs(x = "HOLC Grade", y = "Life Expectancy Percentile", title = "Life Expectancy Percentile by HOLC Grade") 
life_exp_plot

# PM2.5
holc_pm25 <- ej_and_holc |> 
    group_by(grade) |> 
    summarize(mean(P_PM25, na.rm = TRUE))
pm25_plot <- ggplot(holc_pm25, aes(x = grade, y = `mean(P_PM25, na.rm = TRUE)`)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
    labs(x = "HOLC Grade", y = "PM2.5 Exposure Percentile", title = "PM2.5 Exposure Percentile by HOLC Grade") 
pm25_plot

# Low income percentile
holc_lowinc <- ej_and_holc |> 
    group_by(grade) |> 
    summarize(mean(P_LOWINCPCT, na.rm = TRUE))
lowinc_plot <- ggplot(holc_lowinc, aes(x = grade, y = `mean(P_LOWINCPCT, na.rm = TRUE)`)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
    labs(x = "HOLC Grade", y = "% Low Income Percentile", title = "Low Income Percentile by HOLC Grade") 
lowinc_plot
```



### (d). Reflection paragraph
Based on these visualizations, it appears that the average (mean) percentile across all three variables (percent low income, percentile for particulate matter 2.5, and percentile for low life expectancy) increases as the grade decreases (i.e. areas with grade "D" will tend to be in a higher percentile for low income %, PM2.5, and low life expectancy than areas with an "A" grade).  This trend is observed similarly across all three variables.  This trend is likely a result of historical redlining, as these visualizations show that "redlined" areas now display a lower average life expectancy, lower average income, and more PM2.5 air pollution.  In this way, the discriminatory legacy of historical redlining persists today through these variables.


## Part 2: Legacy of redlining in pedstrian and bike accidents
### (a).  Figure summarizing the percent of observations within redlined neighborhoods within each HOLC grade

```{r}
# We need to join the HOLC data with the crashes data
# "Crashes" is not spatial data, so we do not need to worry about CRS matching

# To join "crashes" to "holc", we need to combine the latitude/longitude columns in "crashes",
# and convert it to a spatial object
# We also need to drop NAs!
crash_clean <- crashes |> 
    filter(!is.na(POINT_X), !is.na(POINT_Y))
latlong <- st_as_sf(crash_clean, coords = c("POINT_X", "POINT_Y"), crs = st_crs(holc))
```
```{r}
# Now we check that the CRS match
if(st_crs(latlong) == st_crs(holc)){
  print("CRS match")
}else{
  print("CRS do not match")
}
```
```{r}
# Finally, we can now join the HOLC and crashes datasets
holc <- st_make_valid(holc)
holc_and_crash <- st_join(latlong, holc, join = st_within)
```

```{r}
# Now that we have joined data, we can visualize
# We can now drop geometry
holc_and_crash <- st_drop_geometry(holc_and_crash)

# First, lets look at the number of crashes within each grade
crash_summ <- holc_and_crash |> 
    count(grade) |> 
    mutate(percentage = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 1))

# Based on this table, it appears that the majority of crashes occur in areas given an "NA" grade
# We may need to drop NAs to make the data cleaner
crash_summ_no_na <- holc_and_crash |> 
    filter(!is.na(grade)) |> 
    count(grade) |> 
    mutate(percentage = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 1))

crash_summ_no_na

# After removing NAs, it seems that the majority (53%) of observations in the "crashes" dataset occur in areas given the HOLC grade "C"
```

```{r}
# Looking specifically at bike crashes
bike_crashes <- holc_and_crash |> 
    filter(BICYCLE_ACCIDENT == "Y")
bike_summ <- bike_crashes |> 
    filter(!is.na(grade)) |> 
    count(grade) |> 
    mutate(percentage = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 1))
bike_summ
```

```{r}
# Looking specifically at pedestrian crashes
ped_crashes <- holc_and_crash |> 
    filter(PEDESTRIAN_ACCIDENT == "Y")
ped_summ <- ped_crashes |> 
    filter(!is.na(grade)) |> 
    count(grade) |> 
    mutate(percentage = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 1))
ped_summ
```

```{r}
# Looking specifically at fatalities
fatal_crashes <- holc_and_crash |> 
    filter(NUMBER_KILLED >= 1.00)
fatal_summ <- fatal_crashes |> 
    filter(!is.na(grade)) |> 
    count(grade) |> 
    mutate(percentage = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 1))
fatal_summ
```

Across all three of these categories (bike crashes, pedestrian crashes, and fatal crashes), the majority of incidents (54%-58%) occur in areas with a HOLC grade of "C", followed by "D" (28%-31%), then "B" (11%-13%) and finally "A" (1%-3%).  Therefore, the number of incidents mostly increases with decreasing grade, with the exception of "C" graded areas, which have a higher number of incidents than "D". 

```{r}
# Now that the data is clear, we can use ggplot to visualize it
# first we need to add crash type identifiers to the tables
# And then combine the summary tables into one table
bike_summ <- bike_summ |> 
    mutate("crash_type" = "Bike")
ped_summ <- ped_summ |> 
    mutate("crash_type" = "Pedestrian")
fatal_summ <- fatal_summ |> 
    mutate("crash_type" = "Fatal")
bike_ped_fatal <- bind_rows(ped_summ, bike_summ, fatal_summ)

# Finally we can plot the data!
crash_plot <- ggplot(bike_ped_fatal, aes(x = grade, y = percentage, color = crash_type)) +
    geom_point() +
    labs(x = "HOLC Grade", y = "Percentage of Crash Incidents", title = "Percentage of 2020-2025 LA Crash Incidents in Each HOLC Grade", color = "Crash Type") 
crash_plot
```
